newsitem.title: UK: British unemployment falls to six-year low.
newsitem.headline: British unemployment falls to six-year low.

text.p: British unemployment fell in January to 6.5 percent, its lowest rate in six years, official figures showed Wednesday, giving the government a welcome boost before spring elections.
The Office for National Statistics said the number of jobless workers fell by 67,800 to 1.82 million, or 6.5 percent of the working population, from 1.88 million in December.
But the official figures also showed earnings growth accelerated at the end of last year, raising the prospect of higher inflation in the future.
Underlying average earnings grew 4.25 percent in December, and November growth was revised up to 4.25 percent from an original estimate of 4.0 percent.
The government welcomed the fall in unemployment and played down worries that higher wages foreshadowed higher prices down the line.
"Performance-related bonuses and overtime largely account for a small rise in average earnings growth," a Treasury official said. "There is no sign of any pickup in wage settlements."

Economists, however, said the higher earnings figures were bad news for the government, and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in particular. He is charged with hitting a tough 2.5 percent inflation target.
"The worst news for the government and (financial) markets is the acceleration in underlying average earnings," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank America.
The figures would probably not lead to higher interest rates before the election, which must be held by May, but would increase pressure for a rise soon after, analysts said.
Earlier Wednesday, Clarke, the country's finance minister, dismissed calls by the Bank of England for higher interest rates.
He told a radio interviewer that the strong pound sterling was having a big deflationary effect on the British economy and said he saw no need for tighter credit.
